rows: GM foods contain, consist of or are produced from genetically modified organisms.
GM foods undergo safety assessment before authorisation.
Assessment considers toxicity, nutritional value and potential allergenicity.
Authorised GM foods should not present a health risk under their approved conditions.
Authorisation should not permit misleading consumers or nutritional disadvantage.
Foods containing or consisting of GMOs require applicable labelling.
Ingredients produced from GMOs may also require GM labelling.
Foods produced with processing aids from GM technology may have different labelling treatment.
A GM-free or non-GM marketing statement does not prove regulatory compliance.
Product conclusions require exact ingredient, authorisation, production method, threshold, label and supply-chain evidence.
Fish and shellfish businesses must apply relevant hygiene and approval requirements.
Live bivalve molluscs are subject to production-area classification and official controls.
Import requirements depend on the product and country of origin.
Some fishery products require freezing controls for parasite risk.
Businesses should manage histamine, biotoxin and microbiological hazards where relevant.
Traceability should identify harvesting, production and distribution information.
Temperature control is important for chilled and frozen fishery products.
Raw-oyster norovirus incidents require coordinated product and public-health management.
A shellfish classification or supplier approval does not prove the safety of a particular batch.
Batch conclusions require species, area, harvest date, purification, temperature, testing, traceability and incident evidence.
Animal-feed businesses are subject to feed-safety and hygiene requirements.
Feed ingredients and additives should be authorised for their intended use where required.
Businesses should identify chemical, microbiological and physical hazards in feed.
Mycotoxins and other contaminants require appropriate controls.
Traceability should identify feed materials, suppliers and customers.
Labelling should provide the information required for safe and informed use.
Feed production and storage should prevent cross-contamination.
Complaints, test failures and incidents should trigger investigation and corrective action.
A feed specification or assurance certificate does not prove the safety of every batch.
Batch conclusions require ingredients, authorisations, process, contaminants, sampling, label, traceability and distribution evidence.
Food irradiation can reduce bacteria and other organisms that cause food poisoning or spoilage.
Irradiation does not make food radioactive.
Only permitted foods and authorised irradiation facilities should be used.
The radiation source and process dose should meet applicable requirements.
Businesses should preserve traceability for irradiated products and ingredients.
Applicable labelling should identify irradiated food or irradiated ingredients.
Irradiation does not replace good hygiene or safe handling.
Process controls should be verified and documented.
An irradiation symbol or supplier statement does not prove that all legal conditions were met.
Product conclusions require food type, facility, source, dose, treatment record, label, traceability and storage evidence.
